Flight log

Mission timeline

Aug 2031

Launch — Cape Canaveral

AETHELON lifts off aboard a heavy-lift vehicle onto a Venus-Earth-Earth-Jupiter gravity-assist trajectory. Solar arrays stay stowed; the spacecraft runs on its radioisotope generator from minute one.

Complete
May 2032

Venus gravity assist

A 3,400 km flyby of Venus bends the trajectory and adds 4.1 km/s, sending the probe back toward Earth for the next kick.

Complete
Oct 2033

Earth gravity assist

Returning home for a slingshot, AETHELON checks out its full instrument suite against the Moon before being flung outward past Mars.

Complete
Mar 2036

Jupiter gravity assist · cruise

The final and largest assist. Jupiter's enormous gravity adds the velocity needed to reach Saturn, and the probe images the Galilean moons in passing.

In progress
Jun 2038

Saturn orbit insertion

A 96-minute main-engine burn slows AETHELON enough for Saturn to capture it into a wide, looping orbit threaded between the rings.

Planned
2038 – 2042

Enceladus science campaign

Twenty-three targeted Enceladus flybys, eleven of them straight through the plume at under 5 km/s, sampling ocean material and sounding the ice shell.

Planned
Sep 2042

Disposal

With propellant spent, the probe is steered into Saturn's atmosphere to burn up — protecting Enceladus' ocean from any chance of contamination.

Planned

Why we go

Four science objectives

OBJ-1

Assess habitability

Measure the ocean's chemistry, pH, salinity and energy sources to determine whether Enceladus' sea can sustain life as we know it.

OBJ-2

Search for biosignatures

Hunt the plume for molecular patterns — amino-acid distributions, lipid chains — that would be difficult to produce without biology.

OBJ-3

Map the ice shell

Use ice-penetrating radar and gravity science to chart the shell's thickness and the conduits that connect ocean to surface.

OBJ-4

Understand the plume

Resolve how the geysers work, how their output varies with Enceladus' orbit, and how they sustain Saturn's vast E-ring.
